title: Political incentives and state subsidy allocation: Evidence from Hungarian municipalities
abstract: Using a comprehensive database on successful and rejected applications for the European Union's Structural and Cohesion Funds between 2004 and 2012 in Hungary, we study which grant types are susceptible to political favoritism and how this is achieved. With fixed-effects and matching estimators we study whether applicants from municipalities with a mayor endorsed by the governing coalition won a higher grant value than applicants where the mayor was affiliated with the opposition. We find limited evidence for such a difference for total grant value, but in cases when the applicant is a public entity or the purpose of the project is construction and, therefore, visible to voters and thus may bring about electoral benefits, we do find effects of 16–21%. The decomposition of the effect suggests that favoritism plays a role both in the application and the decision making process as applicants from aligned townships apply in larger numbers and have higher acceptance rates. When analyzing the effect of grants on votes, we show that voters indeed reward construction and public projects but not the other grant types.
summary_en: Are EU Structural and Cohesion Fund grants in Hungary subject to political favouritism? Murakozy and Telegdy use a comprehensive Hungarian database of successful and rejected grant applications 2004-2012, comparing applicants in municipalities with mayors aligned with the governing coalition vs. opposition. Average grant value shows little systematic difference. But for grants visible to voters — public-entity applicants and construction projects — aligned municipalities receive 16-21% higher grant values, driven by both higher application rates and higher acceptance rates. Voters reward construction and public projects with electoral support, justifying the political incentive structure.
data_used: Hungarian administrative data on all successful and rejected applications for EU Structural and Cohesion Funds 2004-2012 (~hundreds of thousands of applications), matched to municipal-level mayoral political affiliation and electoral outcomes.
policy_relevance: Direct political-economy evidence for ÁSZ (State Audit Office), GVH, and EU Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) when assessing Hungarian fund-allocation governance. Documents quantitatively significant favouritism in visible-spending categories. Useful framework for designing transparent grant-allocation procedures and for the European Commission's rule-of-law conditionality dialogue with Hungary.
